## Where This Chapter Fits

Isaiah 36–39 is a block of **prose narrative** set among chapters of prophetic poetry. It closes the first major part of the book (chs. 1–39, set in the 8th century BC). Chapters 36–37 tell of Assyria's threat to Jerusalem and the city's deliverance. Chapters 38–39 tell of Hezekiah's illness and the visit of envoys from Babylon, which looks ahead to the Babylonian setting of chapters 40–66. Chapter 37 is the resolution of the crisis that chapter 36 sets up: the Assyrian field commander has just stood outside Jerusalem's walls and mocked Hezekiah's trust in the LORD.

These same events appear almost word for word in **2 Kings 18:13–19:37** and in shorter form in **2 Chronicles 32**. Scholars debate which version is earlier. Most think the Isaiah form was adapted from (or shares a source with) the Kings account.

## Date and Historical Setting: 701 BC

This is one of the best-documented events in the Old Testament.

- **The empire:** Assyria, ruled from Nineveh, dominated the Near East. In 722 BC it had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel (Samaria).
- **The rebellion:** After the Assyrian king Sargon II died in 705 BC, **Hezekiah** of Judah joined a coalition withholding tribute, with hope of Egyptian support. He prepared Jerusalem for siege, including a water tunnel (2 Kings 20:20) that still survives, along with the Siloam Inscription carved inside it.
- **The campaign:** In **701 BC**, King **Sennacherib** (reigned 705–681 BC) marched west on his "third campaign." His own annals, preserved on clay prisms, claim he captured **46** of Hezekiah's fortified cities, deported many people, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage." The annals record heavy tribute (compare 2 Kings 18:14–16) but **do not claim that Jerusalem was taken**, which is unusual for Assyrian royal boasting.
- **Lachish:** The siege of Lachish, Judah's second city (see v. 8), was carved in stone reliefs on Sennacherib's palace walls at Nineveh, now in the British Museum. Excavations at Lachish confirm a violent destruction at this time.

**A dating puzzle:** Isaiah 36:1 places the invasion in Hezekiah's **14th year**. If 701 BC was his 14th year, he came to the throne around 715 BC. That date conflicts with other synchronisms in 2 Kings 18:1, 9–10, which suggest an earlier accession around 727 BC. Proposed solutions include a co-regency with his father Ahaz or a copying error.

## People and Places

- **Hezekiah:** king of Judah, praised in 2 Kings 18:5 for unmatched trust in the LORD. A clay seal impression reading "belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah" was found in excavations in Jerusalem and published in 2015.
- **Isaiah son of Amoz:** prophet in Jerusalem, active c. 740–700 BC, with access to the royal court.
- **Eliakim and Shebna** (v. 2): senior court officials. Isaiah 22:15–25 records an oracle demoting Shebna and elevating Eliakim.
- **Rabshakeh:** not a personal name but an Assyrian title (*rab-šāqê*, roughly "chief cupbearer"), a high-ranking official.
- **Tirhakah, "king of Ethiopia"** (v. 9): Taharqa of the Nubian (Kushite) 25th Dynasty, which ruled Egypt. He became king in 690 BC, so in 701 he was likely a prince or military commander; the narrator uses the title he later held. Assyrian records confirm a battle against an Egyptian-Kushite force at Eltekeh during this campaign.
- **Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Eden, Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivah** (vv. 12–13): cities and peoples previously conquered by Assyria, cited to argue that no god had ever stopped Assyria.
- **Nisroch** (v. 38): an unidentified Assyrian god. The name may be a garbled form of Nusku or Ninurta.

## The Outcome (vv. 36–38)

The text attributes Assyria's withdrawal to the **angel of the LORD** striking 185,000 men in the camp. No Assyrian source mentions a disaster, which is unsurprising because royal annals did not record defeats. The Greek historian **Herodotus** (5th century BC) preserves an Egyptian tradition that mice swarmed Sennacherib's army and gnawed their bowstrings, which some read as a memory of plague. However the event is explained, the historical facts agree: Sennacherib went home, and Jerusalem was not captured.

Verse 38 compresses about **20 years**. Sennacherib was assassinated in **681 BC** by a son. Babylonian and Assyrian sources confirm the murder and that another son, **Esarhaddon**, succeeded him. Assyriologists identify "Adrammelech" with the crown prince Arda-Mulissu (Urad-Mullissu).

## Theological Setting

The episode became central to **Zion theology**, the conviction that God would defend Jerusalem "for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" (v. 35; see the Davidic covenant in 2 Samuel 7). Over a century later, that confidence hardened into a belief that the temple guaranteed the city's safety. Jeremiah challenged that assumption (Jer. 7; 26), and Lehi was among the prophets who warned that Jerusalem would fall (1 Nephi 1:4, 13, 18–20) before Babylon destroyed the city in 586 BC.

## Restoration Connections

- The **brass plates** carried by Lehi's family contained Isaiah's writings, and Nephi quotes Isaiah extensively (1 Nephi 20–21; 2 Nephi 7–8, 12–24). Isaiah 36–39 is not among the chapters quoted.
- Nephi explains that Isaiah is hard to understand without knowing "the manner of prophesying among the Jews" and "the regions round about" (2 Nephi 25:1–6). This chapter, full of places, rulers, and diplomatic exchanges, shows why that historical knowledge matters.
- The promise that a **remnant** of Judah would "take root downward, and bear fruit upward" (vv. 31–32) anticipates a theme the Book of Mormon develops at length: the preservation and future gathering of a remnant of Israel.

breakdown.title: Hezekiah Mourns and Sends to Isaiah
breakdown.summary: After hearing the Rabshakeh's threats (ch. 36), Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes to the temple. He sends Eliakim, Shebna, and the elder priests to ask Isaiah to pray for the remnant, since Assyria has mocked *the living God*.

breakdown.title: Isaiah's First Oracle: Do Not Fear
breakdown.summary: Isaiah answers that the LORD has heard the blasphemy. Sennacherib will hear a rumor, return home, and fall by the sword in his own land.

breakdown.title: Sennacherib's Letter
breakdown.summary: The Rabshakeh rejoins the king, who has moved from Lachish to Libnah. Hearing that Tirhakah is advancing, Sennacherib sends Hezekiah a written warning: no god of any nation Assyria conquered was able to save it, so Hezekiah should not trust his.

breakdown.title: Hezekiah's Prayer in the Temple
breakdown.summary: Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays. He confesses the LORD as the only God and Creator, admits that Assyria has destroyed nations whose gods were man-made, and asks for deliverance so that all kingdoms may know the LORD alone is God.

breakdown.title: The Taunt Song Against Sennacherib
breakdown.summary: Through Isaiah, the LORD answers in poetry: the *virgin daughter of Zion* mocks the Assyrian king. His boasts of conquest were only what God had long ago ordained, and God will put a hook in his nose and turn him back the way he came.

breakdown.title: A Sign for Hezekiah
breakdown.summary: Judah will eat what grows on its own for two years and plant again in the third. The surviving remnant will take root downward and bear fruit upward, through the zeal of the LORD of hosts.

breakdown.title: The City Will Not Be Taken
breakdown.summary: The LORD promises that the Assyrian king will not enter Jerusalem, shoot an arrow there, or build a siege ramp. God will defend the city for his own sake and for David's sake.

breakdown.title: Deliverance and Sennacherib's End
breakdown.summary: The angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. Years later his sons assassinate him while he worships his god, and Esarhaddon reigns in his place, fulfilling v. 7.

37.literaryUnit:
## Genre

Isaiah 37 is **prophetic historical narrative**: prose storytelling built around three embedded speeches. Two are oracles from Isaiah and one is a royal prayer. The longest oracle (vv. 22–29) is **poetry**, a taunt song directed at an enemy king. The chapter mixes three genres:

- **Narrative** (vv. 1–2, 5, 8–9, 14–15, 21, 36–38), including messenger speeches (vv. 3–4, 10–13)
- **Prayer** (vv. 16–20)
- **Prophetic poetry and oracle** (vv. 6–7, 22–35)

## The Larger Unit

Chapter 37 is the second half of a single story that begins at 36:1 and ends at 37:38. Chapter 36 sets up the threat: the Rabshakeh's speech asks, in effect, "On whom do you trust?" Chapter 37 answers with the LORD's response. The block of chapters 36–39 sits between the Assyrian-era prophecies (chs. 1–35) and the Babylonian-era prophecies (chs. 40–66), and works as a hinge between them.

## A Double Cycle

The chapter tells the same pattern **twice**:

- **Cycle 1 (36:1–37:7):** Assyrian threat delivered by speech → Hezekiah goes to the temple → envoys sent to Isaiah → short oracle
- **Cycle 2 (37:8–35):** Assyrian threat delivered by letter → Hezekiah goes to the temple and prays himself → Isaiah sends a long oracle

Since Stade (1886), many scholars have explained this doubling as two originally separate accounts, often labeled "B1" and "B2," woven together. Read as it stands, the repetition creates **escalation**. The threat moves from spoken word to written document. Hezekiah moves from sending others to pray to praying himself. God's answer grows from three verses to fifteen.

## Prophecy and Fulfillment Frame

Isaiah's first oracle (v. 7) makes three predictions: Sennacherib will hear a rumor, return to his land, and fall by the sword there. The chapter's last verses (vv. 37–38) fulfill each one in order. This **prophecy-fulfillment bracket** frames everything in between.

## Hezekiah's Prayer (vv. 16–20)

The prayer follows a classic shape:

1. **Invocation** naming God as enthroned above the cherubim, the only God, and Creator (v. 16)
2. **Petition to hear and see** (v. 17)
3. **Acknowledgment of the facts:** the conquered nations' gods were "no gods" but wood and stone (vv. 18–19)
4. **Petition with purpose:** "save us… that all the kingdoms of the earth may know" (v. 20)

The prayer answers Assyria's argument directly. Assyria had said that the gods of the nations could not save them. Hezekiah agrees, because those were not real gods, and asks the living God to prove the difference.

## The Taunt Song (vv. 22–29)

- **Personification:** Jerusalem is the *virgin daughter of Zion* who laughs and shakes her head at the invader. The besieged city is pictured as an unconquered young woman scorning a would-be assailant.
- **Quoting the enemy:** vv. 24–25 put Sennacherib's boasts in his own mouth (chariots on mountain heights, cutting cedars of Lebanon, drying up rivers). The images closely match the style of real Assyrian royal inscriptions.
- **Reversal:** God's reply (vv. 26–29) recasts the king's conquests as God's long-planned purpose. The proud king becomes a beast led by a **hook in the nose and a bridle in the lips**, a fitting reversal, since Assyrian art shows captives led by ropes and rings.
- **Meter:** Much of the poem uses the uneven, "limping" 3+2 rhythm (*qinah*) associated with laments, turned here into mockery.

## Key Words and Motifs

- **"Reproach"** (vv. 4, 17, 23, 24): Assyria's taunting of the living God is the charge God answers.
- **"Living God" vs. "no gods"** (vv. 4, 17, 19): the central theological contrast.
- **"Hand"**: "deliver… out of the hand of" Assyria (36:15, 18–20; 37:20) and gods that were the work of men's hands (v. 19).
- **"The way he came"** (vv. 29, 34): repeated to promise a complete reversal of the invasion route.
- **"Remnant"** (vv. 4, 31, 32): what Hezekiah prays for in v. 4 is what God promises in vv. 31–32.

## An Echo of Isaiah 7

The Rabshakeh stands by "the conduit of the upper pool" on the road to the fuller's field (36:2). This is exactly where Isaiah had confronted Hezekiah's father **Ahaz** decades earlier (7:3). Ahaz refused to trust God and sought Assyria's help; Hezekiah, at the same spot, turns to the LORD. The book invites readers to compare the two kings.
